new_entities.name: Paternal age above 45 years
new_entities.description: Father age in the advanced range above about 45 years at the time of conception or birth.

new_entities.name: Autism risk in offspring
new_entities.description: Risk of autism spectrum disorder diagnosed in the child or offspring.

edges.effect_quant: The signal is consistent across large registry cohorts. The Swedish birth cohort found a 2.2-fold autism risk for offspring of fathers aged 50 years or older versus 29 years or younger, while the earlier Israeli cohort found a 5.75-fold risk for fathers 40 years or older versus younger than 30 in a more selected sample. Kaiser Permanente registry data also showed a 28% higher autism risk per 10-year paternal age increase.
edges.population: children born to older fathers in population-based birth and health-register cohorts
edges.mechanism: Advanced paternal age is plausibly linked to accumulating de novo germline mutations and age-related epigenetic drift in sperm. The epidemiology does not prove mechanism, but the persistence of the association across large cohorts makes a purely artifactual explanation harder to defend.
edges.summary: The safest reading is that older paternal age is a genuine autism-risk signal, though the exact magnitude depends on cohort design and comparison group. This is not a deterministic edge, but it is strong enough that a harmful direction is more defensible than a neutral one.
edges.caveats: Absolute autism risk remains low, and paternal age is entangled with maternal age, parity, and family-level social factors. Thresholds also vary across studies, so the above-45 slug should be read as an approximate advanced-age zone rather than a magic cutoff.

evidence.citation: Hultman CM et al 2011 Mol Psychiatry
evidence.notes: Advancing paternal age and risk of autism: new evidence from a population-based study and a meta-analysis of epidemiological studies.
